Great to see you have an entrepreneurial mindset, but you are trying to solve a minor problem from the wrong direction, man. 

First of all, let me poke an obvious hole in your math. If I can buy brand new furniture for $760, and if it costs $1,200 to hire movers to move it, then if I had to move, I would call Goodwill to pick up my furniture for free and then buy new furniture for another $760. Under no circumstances is it rational for someone to pay more to move something from place to place than it would cost to buy a new version of that thing. 

You are marketing a service to a demographic that doesn't exist. People who are moving nearly every year are almost certainly younger and with less disposable income. These people *do not hire movers*. Paying for convenience isn't a concept because they can't afford it. People who are willing and able to pay for movers likely don't move all that often and have more valuable belongings, meaning that they would prefer *their own belongings*, not rentals.

I also want to address your assertion that it is a generational thing that young people move around so much ... it's not. People 22-30 move around, sure, but as people get older, they naturally settle into careers and living situations that are, in general, more stable. To be clear, though, there is not an entire generation of people who routinely move every 1-2 years as a matter of course. When my friends and I got out of college, most of us moved at least once a year... eight years later, my only friends and family who have moved in the past year have a) moved cities due to job relocation, b) purchased homes or c) gotten married/divorced. It just isn't reasonable to expect that people will use your service, were it to exist, for more than a few years before they are in a stable situation.

First, I'm going to answer your questions. Then, I'm going to give you advice. Please bear with me.

> Question: assume I moved overseas...tomorrow? Next week? and moved to a small town in EU? Anywhere. What are the legal consequences of me leaving my child behind, unannounced.

If you're the kid's only form of support and you walk away, then you could easily face extraditable criminal charges, meaning that you may be shipped home by whatever country you move to so that you can face the music. A conviction for child neglect may also make it hard to obtain citizenship or permanent residence in another country for years afterwards.

If you leave your kid in your partner's care, then you are not neglecting them. If you leave your kid in someone else's care, you are still responsible if they fall short.

Moving to another country is not as simple as upping sticks and getting on a plane. You need a visa, which takes time, and generally you need some legal justification for why one should be issued, such as schooling or work, which means you may not be able to start the visa process yet. If you immigrate without a visa, you can be deported if and when the authorities find you.

> I also know that most EU countries offer reciprocal child support enforcement laws that can be enforced upon their residents. How much are these treaties enforced?

Most EU countries actively enforce support child welfare treaties.

> Can he/she go to court and say I abandoned my child without notification and strip me of my rights to see him/her again till my child is 18 years old? 

If you flee to another country and remain there for an extended period (months, at least), then yes, your coparent has a good argument that you abandoned your kid. That may mean you lose your parental rights outright if they and their future partner want to adopt your kid, or that you need to start from zero to re-establish visitation and custody if you ever move back.

> Will I have rights to visitation?

You will have to seek that through the courts where your child lives, and moving out of country without a plan or any communication will count against you. In particular, you can assume that you _cannot_ bring your kid with you out of the country, once you pull a stunt like that: the courts will tend to view you as a very high risk for parental kidnapping.

> Have other's done this? Is there a checklist of steps to take?

It's more common to flee the country to try to avoid child support, and even that's not very effective.

Here's where the _advice_ starts: that's the abuse brain talking. This is a grandiose plan that, superficially, appears to solve your problems, but actually creates more new problems than it actually solves.

**Please contact a local domestic abuse shelter and get out of your ex's home.**

You can move out of your ex's home and bring your kid with you, up to the limits of your current custody decree. Staying in the jurisdiction and making sure your kid is cared for and looked after are good ideas, and will help your case as you seek to amend custody. Even if you opt to leave your kid behind, _you can still leave_ without having to travel to another country.

Domestic abuse groups see people in your state all the time: fear that your partner will keep pursuing you, keep pushing you, and keep abusing you is _normal_. One of the first things a shelter can do is handle your mail, so that you never have to see your ex again even as you sort this out. Many shelters prioritize women, unfortunately, but there are shelters out there for husbands and ex-husbands of abusive wives. Whatever your gender and situation, you can get help.

Once you are out of your ex-partner's sphere of influence, get into intensive personal counselling. Rebuilding your sense of self and your boundaries is as much an appropriate medical intervention after abuse as casting your leg would be if you broke it, and in any case, you deserve the support.

If you already live apart from your ex, then your next step is to restrict all communication to writing, through something recorded and moderated. That could be a PO box you check once a week, or a platform like OurFamilyWizard. Unless your custody orders require it, you never have to speak to your ex or answer the phone, nor do you have to put up with texts, emails, facebook messages, or any other intrusions on your life.

Physically distancing yourself from your ex, and cutting communication down to the narrowest possible channels, also means that it will be much, much harder for them to manufacture legal trouble for you. They can't argue you assaulted them if you haven't been in the same room as them in months, for example, or that you're stalking them if you never visit their home.

Did you by any chance sign up for a third-party energy supplier? They're ~technically~ legitimate in NY, but really scummy. She wasn't an authorized user on our electric co. account, but the 3rd-party supplier lied to them about getting permission from an authorized user. It was ~technically~ legal, again - NY law iirc allows for any resident of a unit to make changes like this to utilities - but it was against the utility co.'s policy. They put a block on my account so that the supplier couldn't switch our service over. (NAL about the NY law thing btw)
